title: Reading News
intro: A late-summer issue: the Summer Reading Challenge is in its final fortnight, this year's big prizes have been handed out, and there's a diary to fill before September.

items.headline: Your most-read author by a distance — and there's plenty more Mildred
items.author: Jill Murphy
items.book: A Bad Spell for the Worst Witch
items.summary: The Worst Witch books are the most-read across our schools this year, with A Bad Spell for the Worst Witch alone logged 34 times. If you have a class hooked, there are eight titles in Penguin's series to work through, and the 50th anniversary clothbound edition of the first book makes a handsome start for a class set.

items.headline: Two more Granny Mutton stories for the children who loved A Box of Socks
items.author: Amanda Brandon
items.summary: A Box of Socks is our second most-read title, and it's the middle of a trio: A Scarf and a Half came first and A Knit and a Knot turns Granny Mutton and Little Lionel into detectives hunting missing wool. Brandon also has two new chapter books out this year, Starship Mystery and The Curse of Raven's Hall, for readers ready to move up from early readers.

items.headline: Michael Morpurgo's memoir arrives next month — and every penny goes to Farms for City Children
items.author: Michael Morpurgo
items.book: In the Mouth of the Wolf
items.summary: Down Burrow Lane: Life and Love on the Farm is published on 17 September by Hodder & Stoughton, fifty years after Michael and Clare Morpurgo moved their family to a Devon farm and started writing. It's a book for grown-ups rather than the class, but the charity behind it may interest you: Farms for City Children has given more than 100,000 children a week in the countryside, and Morpurgo is donating all the proceeds to it.

items.headline: Seventeen Roman Mysteries, and your readers are only ten in
items.author: Caroline Lawrence
items.summary: The Enemies of Jupiter is book ten of seventeen, so anyone gripped by it has a long way still to run. Lawrence describes it as "Nancy Drew in Ancient Rome" — her heroine Flavia Gemina is ten when the series starts — and ten of the seventeen were televised by the BBC. A useful bridge for primary readers who want history that moves like a thriller.

items.headline: A picture book about dyslexia takes this year's Carnegie Illustration Medal
items.author: Kate Rolfe
items.summary: Wiggling Words (Two Hoots) won the Carnegie Medal for Illustration on 23 June. Rolfe draws her own dyslexia from the inside, using typography and colour to show both the struggle with words on a page and the creative thinking that came with it. One to have on the shelf for any child who has decided reading isn't for them.

items.headline: Waterstones Children's Book Prize goes to a bedtime story about a blob
items.author: Huw Aaron
items.summary: Sleep Tight, Disgusting Blob (Puffin) took both Best Illustrated Book and the overall prize — a cosy, rhyming spin on all things spooky. For slightly older readers, Evie and Maryam's Family Tree by Janeen Hyat (Guppy Books) won Best Book for Younger Readers.

events.name: Summer Reading Challenge ends
events.blurb: This year's challenge is Read to the Beat, all about the link between stories and songs. It finishes on 31 August at most library services, so there's still time to nudge families to get their last books counted.

events.name: Roald Dahl Day — his 110th birthday
events.blurb: Dahl was born on 13 September 1916, so this is the 110th. Worth noting it lands on a Sunday this year, so most schools will mark it on the Friday before or the Monday after.

events.name: National Poetry Day
events.blurb: This year's theme is Wonder, with Michael Rosen and Hot Poets exploring climate and nature through poetry. Classroom resources go up on the National Literacy Trust site in the weeks beforehand.

events.name: Michael Morpurgo's birthday
events.blurb: Born in 1943, and one of the most-read authors across our schools. A good excuse to put War Horse or Friend or Foe in front of a class that hasn't met him yet.

events.name: World Book Day 2027
events.blurb: Always the first Thursday in March. A long way off, but it has a habit of arriving the week you meant to start planning it.

general.label: Reading research
general.text: Children's reading enjoyment has risen for the first time in five years: 36.1% of 8 to 18-year-olds say they enjoy reading in their free time, up from 32.7% in 2025.
general.source: National Literacy Trust, Annual Literacy Survey 2026

general.label: Did you know?
general.text: One in five children (20.3%) now read daily in their own time, up from 18.7% the year before — the first increase in daily reading since 2023.
general.source: National Literacy Trust, Annual Literacy Survey 2026

general.label: Worth knowing
general.text: The picture is different at primary age: enjoyment among 5 to 8-year-olds slipped slightly, from 62.6% to 61.6%, with the fall driven by boys. Still high — but the one age group heading the wrong way.
general.source: National Literacy Trust, Annual Literacy Survey 2026

general.label: Reading news
general.text: This summer's library challenge, Read to the Beat, was run with Universal Music UK and asked children to explore how stories and songs both spark imagination. Free to join at any public library.
